ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Johnny Cash — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care new-patient visit for diabetes, lightheadedness on standing, and glaucoma follow-up

text.paragraph: Primary care new-patient visit for diabetes, lightheadedness on standing, and glaucoma follow-up [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Lightheaded when he stands and afraid of another fall; was once told he had Shy-Drager syndrome and wants to know what he really has. [S]
Wants to keep the sight he has left so he can keep writing songs. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: J. R. (Johnny) Cash was born on February 26, 1932, in Kingsland, Cleveland County, Arkansas, to Ray and Carrie Cash. [D]
Cash's older brother Jack died in a sawmill accident in 1944. [D]

In 1957 Cash began taking amphetamines to stay awake on a long road trip, the start of an addiction that lasted about a decade; in a 2002 interview he named amphetamines and barbiturates in the 1960s. [D]
Cash was hospitalized in 1983 with internal bleeding; after recovering he entered the Betty Ford Clinic for treatment. [D]
In October 1997 Cash was diagnosed with Shy-Drager syndrome, an illness similar to Parkinson's disease; in a 2000 interview he said the diagnosis was a misdiagnosis. [D]

Cash later learned he had autonomic neuropathy; in November 2002 he described it as a deadening of the nerve endings in his lower extremities that had taken the strength from his legs, so that he could walk, but not very well. [D]

Cash was repeatedly hospitalized for pneumonia in his last years; he was treated for pneumonia at Baptist Hospital in Nashville in February 2001, and in November 2002 he said he had had pneumonia four times in three years. [D]
In November 2002 Cash said about 60 percent of his vision was gone, which he attributed to the neuropathy and the diabetes, and he said he hoped the glaucoma could also be reversed. [D]

code.displayName: Physical findings of General status Narrative

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Orthostatic vital signs at intake: 146/80 seated and 112/68 after three minutes standing, heart rate 78 to 82; lightheaded on standing and two falls in six months. Walks with a cane; reduced vibration and monofilament sensation to the ankles in both feet; independent in basic activities of daily living. Low vision from advanced glaucoma: tunnel vision in both eyes and difficulty in dim light; no longer drives. [S]

Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily and set an individualized HbA1c goal below 7.5%; avoid insulin and sulfonylureas while autonomic neuropathy may blunt warning symptoms of hypoglycemia. Guideline: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, diabetes, glaucoma, and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Endocrinology consultation to confirm diabetic autonomic neuropathy as the cause of orthostatic hypotension, reconsider the earlier Shy-Drager label, and choose add-on glucose-lowering therapy. Guideline: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 (2025) [S]

Treat neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: stand up in stages, raise the head of the bed, use waist-high compression, drink 2 liters of fluid a day, then midodrine with the last dose at least four hours before bed; check supine blood pressure at each visit. Guideline: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 (2025) [S]

Check HbA1c every three months until at goal, a basic metabolic panel, UACR, and lipids each year, lipids 4 to 12 weeks after starting a statin, and vitamin B12 periodically on metformin. Guideline: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, diabetes, glaucoma, and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Examine the feet at every visit because of sensory loss; daily self-inspection and protective footwear. Guideline: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, diabetes, glaucoma, and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Coordinate glaucoma care with the eye clinic: add dorzolamide to latanoprost, check pressure at each visit, and repeat OCT and visual fields every six months; avoid timolol and brimonidine because of bradycardia, bronchospasm, and low blood pressure. Guideline: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, diabetes, glaucoma, and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Annual dilated eye examination for diabetic retinopathy; low-vision rehabilitation and home lighting review. Guideline: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 (2025); Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern (2025) [S]
Start atorvastatin 40 mg; give PCV20 and recombinant zoster vaccines. Guideline: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 (2025) [S]
